title: Training-Time Law
summary: Apply the training-time law to identify utilization as the immediate profiling target when workload size and peak-throughput convention are fixed.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Training-Time Law** in *Model Training* (Vol I). By the end you should be able to:

- Apply the training-time law to identify utilization as the immediate profiling target when workload size and peak-throughput convention are fixed
- Classify mixed-precision training by its direct target term ($R_{\text{peak}}$) in the training-time law
- Explain what the simplified training-time law captures and why it does not by itself localize the cause of low-throughput execution
- Distinguish compute-bound dense training from regimes where memory capacity or bandwidth is the limiting constraint
- Trace the historical sequence linking major training-system milestones to the constraints they exposed

blocks.source: Vol I, Model Training, § Training-Time Law
blocks.md: Every later estimate in the chapter starts from how long the run takes, and the training-time law fixes that first. GPT-2 XL's run needs about …. Converting that operation count into days on an accelerator, and every loss of time into a factor engineering can recover, requires splitting training time into physical factors, with every wasted second showing up as a lower utilization factor.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md: Pay attention to: applying the training-time law to measured telemetry; mapping optimizations to O, R_peak, and eta_hw; scope conditions and failure modes of the simplified Iron Law; workload characterization (dense compute-bound GPT-2 vs memory-bound DLRM).

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain the scope conditions under which the simplified training-time law $T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$ is useful, and identify why the formula alone cannot diagnose a slow small-batch debugging run.
blocks.md: The equation is useful as an accounting identity: it relates total work, a chosen peak-throughput reference, and effective achieved throughput into one training-time estimate. But because the end-to-end utilization term can already include stalls from launches, transfers, synchronization, and underfilled kernels, the formula alone does not reveal which mechanism caused a slow run. In a small-batch debug session, the problem is not that the law becomes invalid; it is that a low measured utilization could come from many overheads, so diagnosis still requires profiling rather than reading the formula by itself.

questions.q: A training run has confirmed that input delivery and communication are off the critical path. The model FLOP count and the peak-throughput convention are being held fixed, yet profiling still reports only 38 percent effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak. Under the training-time law $T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$, which lever is the most direct target for the next round of profiling?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. In the current equation, $O$ and the chosen $R_{\text{peak}}$ convention are fixed, so 38 percent effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak points to the effective utilization term $\eta_{\text{hw}}$. That does not prove one unique cause, but it does justify profiling device execution for stalls, inefficient kernels, launch overhead, or other losses inside the end-to-end throughput term. Reducing $O$ may shorten total training time, but it answers a different question than why this execution reaches only 38 percent of the chosen peak.
questions.hint: Think about: apply the training-time law to identify utilization as the immediate profiling target when workload size and peak-throughput convention are fixed.
options: Hardware utilization $\eta_{\text{hw}}$, because with $O$ and the relevant $R_{\text{peak}}$ convention fixed, the remaining gap points to how efficiently kernels are being executed end to end.
Peak throughput $R_{\text{peak}}$, because low effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak automatically means the hardware peak specification is too small for the workload.
Total operations $O$, because once data and communication are hidden, utilization is no longer relevant to training time.
Dataset size, because shrinking the number of tokens directly raises effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak even when execution efficiency is unchanged.

questions.q: When a team transitions a model from FP32 training to mixed-precision (FP16/BF16) on Tensor Core accelerators without changing the model architecture, batch size, or dataset, which term of the training-time law ($T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$) is most directly improved?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. The chapter's optimization matching table assigns mixed precision (FP16/BF16) to peak throughput ($R_{\text{peak}}$). Tensor Cores execute reduced-precision matrix multiplications at several times the theoretical FLOP/s ceiling of FP32 ALUs. The claim regarding total operations $O$ is incorrect because the algorithmic graph and number of multiply-accumulate operations remain identical. The utilization claim is incorrect because $\eta_{\text{hw}}$ measures efficiency relative to the available peak, and precision changes do not inherently eliminate data loader bubbles. The data volume claim is false because precision does not reduce sample requirements.
questions.hint: Think about: classify mixed-precision training by its direct target term ($R_{\text{peak}}$) in the training-time law.
options: Total operations $O$, because lower numerical precision halves the number of multiplications required in each matrix multiplication.
Hardware utilization $\eta_{\text{hw}}$, because mixed precision automatically eliminates all GPU pipeline bubbles and CPU data stalls.
Peak throughput $R_{\text{peak}}$, because Tensor Cores provide a substantially higher theoretical FLOP/s ceiling for reduced-precision matrix operations compared to standard FP32 execution units.
Data volume $D_{\text{tokens}}$, because lower precision requires fewer training tokens for the loss to converge.

questions.q: All large deep learning models are primarily compute-bound, so training speed is always governed mainly by Tensor Core TFLOP/s.
questions.explanation: False. Dense transformer training often spends much of its work in matrix multiplications, but other workloads can be limited by memory capacity or bandwidth instead. The section's DLRM example is dominated by large embedding tables, where fitting and moving the state can matter more than raw dense-math throughput.
questions.hint: Think about: distinguish compute-bound dense training from regimes where memory capacity or bandwidth is the limiting constraint.

questions.q: Place the following milestones in chronological order, reflecting how training-system constraints evolved:
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (2) Backpropagation is popularized for multilayer neural networks, (4) AlexNet demonstrates that deep neural network training maps effectively to GPUs, (1) Transformers shift sequence modeling toward high-throughput dense matrix multiplication and large activation footprints, (3) Large-scale foundation models such as GPT-3 make utilization and multi-accelerator scaling central engineering concerns, (5) IO-aware FlashAttention appears as a response to attention memory-bandwidth limits. This sequence matters because each later systems response addresses a constraint exposed by the earlier stage: GPU acceleration follows practical deep learning, transformers amplify activation and attention costs, frontier-scale models make utilization and scaling decisive, and FlashAttention targets the resulting IO bottleneck in attention.
questions.hint: Think about: trace the historical sequence linking major training-system milestones to the constraints they exposed.
items: Backpropagation is popularized for multilayer neural networks.
AlexNet demonstrates that deep neural network training maps effectively to GPUs.
Transformers shift sequence modeling toward high-throughput dense matrix multiplication and large activation footprints.
Large-scale foundation models such as GPT-3 make utilization and multi-accelerator scaling central engineering concerns.
IO-aware FlashAttention appears as a response to attention memory-bandwidth limits.

points: You can now apply the training-time law to identify utilization as the immediate profiling target when workload size and peak-throughput convention are fixed.
You can now classify mixed-precision training by its direct target term ($R_{\text{peak}}$) in the training-time law.
You can now explain what the simplified training-time law captures and why it does not by itself localize the cause of low-throughput execution.
You can now distinguish compute-bound dense training from regimes where memory capacity or bandwidth is the limiting constraint.
